Query: HTTP header injection prevention techniques - To prevent HTTP header injection, you can follow these techniques:

1. Sanitize Input:
   - Validate and sanitize user input before using it to set HTTP headers. Ensure that the input does not contain any newline characters or other special characters that could be used for injection.

2. Use Proper Encoding:
   - Encode any user input that is being used to set HTTP headers. For example, use encoding functions like `encodeURIComponent()` in JavaScript to encode the input before setting it in the header.

3. Limit Input Length:
   - Limit the length of user input that is being used to set HTTP headers. This can help prevent attackers from injecting long strings that could potentially disrupt the header structure.

4. Use a Whitelist Approach:
   - Instead of trying to filter out specific characters, use a whitelist approach where you only allow known safe characters in the input for setting HTTP headers.

5. Implement Content Security Policy (CSP):
   - Implementing Content Security Policy headers can help mitigate the risk of HTTP header injection by specifying which sources are allowed to be used for different types of content.

By following these techniques, you can reduce the risk of HTTP header injection vulnerabilities in your application.

Supporting Fact: HTTP header injection prevention techniques - In HTTP, "Referer" (a misspelling of "Referrer") is an optional HTTP header field that identifies the address of the web page (i.e., the URI or IRI) from which the resource has been requested. By checking the referrer, the server providing the new web page can see where the request originated.
In the most common situation, this means that when a user clicks a hyperlink in a web browser, causing the browser to send a request to the server holding the destination web page, the request may include the Referer field, which indicates the last page the user was on (the one where they clicked the link).
Web sites and web servers log the content of the received Referer field to identify the web page from which the user followed a link, for promotional or statistical purposes. This entails a loss of privacy for the user and may introduce a security risk. To mitigate security risks, browsers have been steadily reducing the amount of information sent in Referer. As of March 2021, by default Chrome, Chromium-based Edge, Firefox, Safari default to sending only the origin in cross-origin requests, stripping out everything but the domain name.

output.description:
To prevent HTTP header injection, consider the following best practices:

1. Sanitize Input: Validate and sanitize all user input before using it to construct HTTP headers. This includes input from forms, query parameters, cookies, and any other user-controlled data.

2. Use Safe Encoding: Use safe encoding methods, such as URL encoding, when constructing headers to ensure that special characters are properly encoded and cannot be interpreted as part of the header.

3. Limit User Input: Limit the length and type of user input that can be used to construct headers to prevent malicious input from being injected.

4. Use a Secure Framework: Use a secure web framework that handles HTTP headers securely and provides built-in protection against header injection attacks.

5. Implement Content Security Policy (CSP): Implement CSP headers to restrict the sources from which certain types of content can be loaded, reducing the risk of malicious content injection.

6. Regularly Update Libraries and Dependencies: Keep all libraries and dependencies up to date to ensure that any known vulnerabilities related to HTTP header injection are patched.

By following these best practices, you can reduce the risk of HTTP header injection attacks and enhance the security of your web application.

output.description:
HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) is a policy mechanism that helps to protect websites against man-in-the-middle attacks such as protocol downgrade attacks and cookie hijacking. It allows web servers to declare that web browsers (or other complying user agents) should automatically interact with it using only HTTPS connections, which provide Transport Layer Security (TLS/SSL), unlike the insecure HTTP used alone. HSTS is an IETF standards track protocol and is specified in RFC 6797.
The HSTS Policy is communicated by the server to the user agent via an HTTP response header field named Strict-Transport-Security. HSTS Policy specifies a period of time during which the user agent should only access the server in a secure fashion.: §5.2  Websites using HSTS often do not accept clear text HTTP, either by rejecting connections over HTTP or systematically redirecting users to HTTPS (though this is not required by the specification). The consequence of this is that a user-agent not capable of doing TLS will not be able to connect to the site.
The protection only applies after a user has visited the site at least once, relying on the principle of "trust on first use". The way this protection works is that when a user entering or selecting an HTTP (not HTTPS) URL to the site, the client, such as a Web browser, will  automatically upgrade to HTTPS without making an HTTP request, thereby preventing any HTTP man-in-the-middle attack from occurring.
